doc_summary: Beth Barnes clarifies that METR has not acted as an auditor, that earlier GPT-4/Claude work was informal pilots rather than meaningful oversight, and that its priority is building the science of evaluations usable by any evaluator. The post is organizational rather than methodological, but it states what it takes for an evaluation to count as credible.

items.claim: Prefers evaluations run with full access to the final deployed model, including the ability to fine-tune, over evaluations on early or partial versions, because results on non-final models cannot support reliable judgments about risky capabilities.
items.quote: As a next step, ARC will need to conduct experiments that (a) involve the final version of the deployed model (b) involve ARC doing its own fine-tuning, before a reliable judgment of the risky emergent capabilities of GPT-4-launch can be made

items.claim: Distrusts informal pilot evaluations done without adequate access as evidence of safety, and refuses to count them as audits or meaningful oversight.
items.quote: Those were informal pilots of what an audit might involve, or research collaborations – not providing meaningful oversight.

items.claim: Prefers evaluations that have formal disclosure rights and a binding link to deployment decisions over NDA-bound, advisory-only evaluations because evidence only counts as oversight if it can inform action.
items.quote: it was all under NDA – we didn’t have any right or responsibility to disclose our findings to anyone outside the labs – and there wasn’t any formal expectation it would inform deployment decisions.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluation results obtained without the access needed for a proper evaluation, since limited access means the model's true capabilities may be understated.
items.quote: We also didn’t have the access necessary to perform a proper evaluation.

items.claim: Prefers developing the science of evaluation protocols that any evaluator can run over becoming an auditor, because the methodology is the bottleneck and is independent of who runs it.
items.quote: We aim to build evaluation protocols that can be used by evaluators/auditors regardless of whether that is the government, an internal lab team, another third party, or a team at METR.

items.claim: Good elicitation requires specific technical expertise, and capability-eval quality depends on elicitation skill, so who runs the evaluation affects how trustworthy the evidence is.
items.quote: Technical considerations of what kind of expertise is required for doing good elicitation.

items.claim: Prefers claiming only what the work supports (pilots, not audits) over implying more oversight than occurred, because overclaiming creates false assurance.
items.quote: METR has not intended to claim to have audited anything, or to claim to be providing meaningful oversight or accountability, but there has been some confusion about whether METR is an auditor or planning to be one.

items.claim: Decides whether to expand into third-party evaluation by conditioning on whether evaluators can perform protocols well and whether it detracts from the science priority.
items.quote: How successful we are in hiring the talent we need to do this without detracting from our top priority of developing the science.

items.claim: Emphasizes that evaluation credibility depends on formal arrangements and access commitments with labs, both for pre-deployment evaluation and for research to improve evaluations.
items.quote: We think it’s important for there to be third-party evaluators with formal arrangements and access commitments - both for evaluating new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed, and for conducting research to improve evaluations.
